# UK Government Analysis Function, the AQuA Book (2025 edition), Warranting Agent-Built Software Distillation

**Source:** UK Government Analysis Function. *The AQuA Book* (the Analytical Quality Assurance Book), 2025 edition, GOV.UK guidance, https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-aqua-book ; first published 2025-07-30 per the operator's source record. No single author; the revised edition was produced by a task and finish group of fourteen named members. Licence: Open Government Licence v3.0; contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0. **Scope:** open. Citations take the form `(Ch N, "Section heading")`.

**Setting, read before projecting.** The AQuA Book is guidance for analysis and models produced for UK government decisions: economic, statistical, actuarial, operational research and similar work, increasingly done in code and increasingly using machine learning and AI. Its *black box models* are AI and other models used *in* the analysis, not coding agents that write software. It says nothing about client contracts, production services, security threats or agents with tools and permissions. What it offers this axis is a mature assurance regime with the shape the axis needs: proportionate assurance set by business risk, a written specification that states the required assurance, an assurer who shall be independent of the analyst, traceable records, and an approver who signs off on the assurance evidence rather than on the work itself. Every step from analysis assurance to agent-built software below is this distillation's own transfer, marked *Transfer:*. The working mapping, also a transfer, is: the **commissioner** is the client who asks for the change; the **analyst** is the build (the coding agent session together with the builder who directs it); the **assurer** is the independent reviewer, agent or human, outside the build; the **approver** is the accountable builder who signs the warranty pack. The book's modal force is kept as it writes it: "shall" is mandatory in all circumstances, "should" is comply-or-explain, "may" is an option, and "must" appears in a few places the book's own list does not define (Ch 1, "1.3 How to use this book").

**Applicability gate (Pass G.0): clear yes.** (1) The source asks the axis's own questions in its own setting: who must assure work that someone else produced, how much assurance a piece of work needs, what the approver signs off on, what to do when time runs out before assurance does, and how to assure a model nobody can see inside. (2) Its roles and stages land on all eight phases, strongest on specifying, triaging risk, reviewing independently and warranting; Phase 4 gets only the record-keeping duties of the analysis stage. (3) Its positions against (assurance as verification alone, assurance out of proportion, interventions taken one at a time, a linear life cycle, the analyst and assurer combined) bear directly on the axis's three reflexes: the assurer's independence answers *the agent says it's done*, the risk responses answer *it worked first time*, and the approver's sign-off on assurance evidence, rather than on the work, answers *I read the diff*.

**Phase mapping.**

| Phase | Fit | What the source brings |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Specifying the change | Strong | Engagement and scoping; a specification signed off by the commissioner that states boundaries, constraints, the acceptable level of risk and the required level of assurance, and agreed accuracy and margins of error; the specification as the reference for later validation |
| 2 Triaging risk | Strong | Proportionality: ten factors (Table 3-1), four interventions that scale and build on each other (Figure 3-1), business risk as effect times likelihood with responses per level (Table 3-3), business-critical work, black-box models under the same structured approach |
| 3 Locking the tests | Moderate | Verification and validation planned at design and reviewed by the assurer before the analysis; tests baselined against independent reference cases; verification of the automatic tests themselves; test suites for module integration; six classes of verification technique |
| 4 Building in the sandbox | Partial | Only the analysis stage's duties: traceable records of assurance, changes, decisions and assumptions shall be produced; design changes raised with the commissioner. Nothing on sandboxing, permissions or agent behaviour |
| 5 Gating deterministically | Moderate | RIGOUR's Repeatable; version control and each run's data and parameters for repeat runs; code practice the analyst shall follow and the assurer shall review; insufficient assurance acknowledged in the assurance statement |
| 6 Reviewing independently | Strong | The assurer shall be independent and the analyst shall still assure; analyst and assurer never combined; the assurer reviews the analyst's assurance, does further verification and validation, reports errors and re-reviews; analyst-assurer separation scaled up to external audit; suitable challenge |
| 7 Warranting the change | Strong | The approver shall review the assurance evidence; the assurance state confirmed; an assurance statement with known limitations; risk responses by level; a single accountable individual per role; user documentation; limits of use and a sunset date |
| 8 Releasing and operating | Moderate | Maintenance and continuous review; regular checks that relied-on software is still supported; model health and drift; sunset date; multi-use models used outside their scope; an open culture when things go wrong |

## Warranting Agent-Built Software Relevance

The AQuA Book answers, for government analysis, the question this axis asks of agent-built software: when the person who signs did not produce the work and cannot inspect all of it, what must be true before they sign? Its answer is a division of labour. The analyst does the work and their own assurance; an assurer, who shall be independent of the analyst, reviews that assurance, does further verification and validation, and confirms to the approver that the work was appropriately scoped, executed, validated, verified and documented; and the approver shall review the assurance evidence and sign off (Ch 5, "5.1 Roles and responsibilities"; Ch 9, "9.1.4 The approver’s responsibilities"). The approver signs on evidence that someone independent assured the work, not on having re-done it. *Transfer:* the accountable builder who does not read every line is in the approver's seat, and the book is clear that the approver's confidence rests on an independent assurer and a record, never on the analyst's own word.

Its second contribution is proportion. The book does not ask for maximum assurance on everything: assurance should be proportionate to the risk of the intended use and the complexity of the method, guided by a structured assessment of business risk, with high risk not to be tolerated and medium risk tolerated only with the commissioner's agreement (Ch 1, "1.3.1 Proportionate assurance"; Ch 3, "3.2 Structured assessment of business risk and complexity"). And it is direct about shortfalls: if time constraints mean insufficient assurance took place, that should be acknowledged in an assurance statement setting out known limitations (Ch 4, "4.2.1 Capacity"). *Transfer:* the warranty pack is the assurance statement, and a pack that hides what was not assured breaks a "should" the book states plainly.

## Key Concepts for Warranting Agent-Built Software

1. <!-- concept: shall-should-may --> **Shall, should, may.** The book defines "shall" as a requirement that "applies in all circumstances and at all times" [V], "should" as a recommendation "to be met on a ‘comply or explain’ basis" [V], and "may" as a good idea that is neither mandatory nor advisory [AP] (Ch 1, "1.3 How to use this book"). Its hard requirements are few and written as "shall": all analysis shall be assured; the assurer and analyst shall be independent and separate in all cases; traceable assurance records shall be produced during analysis; all analysis shall have user documentation; the analyst shall follow good code practice proportionately and the assurer shall review it; the approver shall review the assurance evidence. *Transfer:* a harness that adopts this regime can carry the same grades, so that a "should" skipped is logged with its explanation and a "shall" skipped blocks.

2. <!-- concept: proportionate-assurance --> **Proportionate assurance, built up rather than swapped.** "Quality assurance effort should be appropriate to the risk associated with the intended use of the analysis and the complexity of the analytical approach." [V] (Ch 1, "1.3.1 Proportionate assurance"). Table 3-1 lists ten factors, among them business criticality, complexity, novelty (an untried method needs more assurance; confidence grows as a technique is repeatedly tested), reuse or repurposing (which may need fresh verification and validation), longevity, and repeat runs [AP] (Ch 3, "3.1 Factors for determining appropriate assurance"). Figure 3-1 scales four interventions with risk and complexity: consultation on methods, use of reproducible pipeline tools, analyst-assurer separation (from analyst-led testing to external audit), and documentation detail; "The interventions in figure 3-1 must not be viewed in isolation. The interventions should build on each other." [V] (Ch 3, "3.1 Factors for determining appropriate assurance"). Over-assurance is also named: it is not necessary to spend months assuring simple analysis with a minor influence on a decision [AP].

3. <!-- concept: business-risk-matrix --> **Business risk as effect times likelihood, with a response per level.** Business risk combines the potential effect of errors with their likelihood, and where risk is high, reducing likelihood matters more than reducing effect, because the effect is usually beyond the analyst's control (Ch 3, "3.2 Structured assessment of business risk and complexity"). Table 3-3: "High risk should not be tolerated." [V], new assurance measures must be considered, then terminating or transferring the risk, and if it must still be tolerated the commissioner should fully understand it; "Medium risk should not be tolerated without the agreement of the commissioner." [V]; "Low risk can be tolerated." [V] (Ch 3, "3.2", Table 3-3). *Transfer:* in software a rollback or a narrower reach can lower the effect of some errors, which the book's setting rarely allows; the book's weighting toward likelihood is a claim about analysis, and the distillation does not carry it over unchanged.

4. <!-- concept: verification-and-validation --> **Verification and validation.** Assurance "is more than checking that the analysis is error-free and satisfies its specification (verification)" [V]; it should also check fitness for the purpose it is used for (validation) (Ch 1, "1.3.3 Verification and validation"). "Validation is testing whether the product meets the requirements of users. It is important to involve the users in the process." [V] (Ch 8, "8.2.1 Verification and validation"). The book passes on six classes of verification technique from prior work it cites [BT]: informal, static, dynamic (unit, integration and stress testing), symbolic, constraint (assertions and boundary analysis) and formal (Ch 8, "8.2.1"). *Transfer:* a green suite verifies the change against what the tests encode; it does not validate that the change does what the client needs.

5. <!-- concept: rigour --> **RIGOUR, the analyst's own questions.** Repeatable, Independent, Grounded in reality, Objective, Uncertainty-managed, Robust (Ch 1, "1.3.5 Analysis with RIGOUR"). Two land hard here. Repeatable: exact matches are not guaranteed, but "repeatability means that if an approach is repeated the results should be as expected" [V]. Objective: effective engagement and suitable challenge reduce the risk of bias [AP] (Ch 1, "1.3.5 Analysis with RIGOUR"). Design assurance asks whether the plan is likely to meet RIGOUR (Ch 7, "7.2 Assurance activities").

6. <!-- concept: four-assurance-roles --> **Four roles, one accountable individual each.** Commissioner, analyst, assurer and approver; each may be a team, but "a single individual (for example, the chair of a committee) will have overall accountability for each role" [V] (Ch 5, "5.1 Roles and responsibilities"). One person may hold several roles on quick or simple work, "apart from the assurer and analyst roles which shall be separate from one another in all cases" [V] (Ch 5, "5.1"). *Transfer:* an agent can do the analyst's or the assurer's work, but the accountability the book places on a single individual has to land on a named person; and the builder who directed the build sits in the analyst role, so they can be the approver but not the assurer.

7. <!-- concept: independent-assurer --> **The independent assurer, on top of the analyst's own assurance.**

> "The roles of analyst and assurer shall be distinct from each other. The analyst should carry out their own assurance but responsibility for formal assurance to the approver and commissioner lies with the assurer."
> (Ch 5, "5.1 Roles and responsibilities")

"The assurer and the analyst shall be independent." [V], with the degree of separation depending on the importance of the output and the size and complexity of the work, and "This does not mean that the analyst should not undertake assurance, rather that there shall also be some formal independent assurance." [V] (Ch 3, "Proportionality"). The assurer reviews the analyst's assurance, carries out further verification and validation as they see fit, reports errors and areas for improvement, re-reviews as required, and should consider whether they are qualified to assure a revised method [AP] (Ch 5, "5.1"; Ch 8, "8.1.3 The assurer’s responsibilities").

8. <!-- concept: specification-states-required-assurance --> **A specification that states the required assurance.** Commissioner and analyst develop "a shared understanding of the problem and the context" [V] (Ch 6, "Engagement and scoping"). The analyst's specification captures the question, context, boundaries, constraints, assumptions, risks and business-criticality; "It should state the acceptable level of risk and the required level of assurance." [V]; the commissioner signs it off (Ch 6, "6.1.2 The analyst’s responsibilities"). The stage should agree the outputs, "including acceptable levels of accuracy, precision and margins of error" [V] (Ch 6, "6.2 Assurance activities"), and the specification is the reference for later validation and the approver's evidence at delivery (Ch 6, "6.3 Documentation").

9. <!-- concept: traceable-assurance-records --> **Traceable records, produced as the work happens.** "Throughout this phase traceable documentation of the assurance activities that have been undertaken shall also be produced." [V] (Ch 5, "5.2.3 Analysis"). The stage includes "maintaining appropriate and traceable records of the analysis and assurance activities conducted, changes, decisions and assumptions made" [V] (Ch 8, "Analysis"). Assumptions and decisions logs record what, when, why, who made it and who signed it off [AP] (Ch 2, "Assumptions log"; "Decisions log"). *Transfer:* this is the change's ledger, and the book makes it a "shall" during the build, not a summary written at the end.

10. <!-- concept: black-box-assurance --> **Black boxes: weight moves to design and to outputs.** Black box models are "defined by their inputs and outputs, without insight into internal workings" [V] (Ch 1, "1.1 The updated version (2025)"). "Using black box models places greater weight on the design of the analysis and the assurance and validation of outputs by domain experts." [V] (Ch 7, "7.5 Black box models"). With them, "the same structured approach to assessing business risk should be taken" [V] (Ch 3, "3.4 Black-box models and business risk"); scoping should discuss ethics and risks to judge whether such a model is appropriate at all (Ch 6, "6.5 Black box models"); design should plan automatic checks that flag unexpected behaviour (Ch 7, "7.5"); and analysis should include verification of the automatic tests that the model behaves as expected (Ch 8, "8.5 Black box models"). *Transfer:* the book means AI models inside the analysis, which matches an LLM call or agent tool inside the client's product directly; for the coding agent itself, only the principle carries (when the process can't be inspected, assurance moves to the specification and to checking outputs).

11. <!-- concept: assurance-statement-and-sign-off --> **The assurance statement and the approver's sign-off.** "If time constraints mean insufficient assurance has taken place this should be explicitly acknowledged and reported in an assurance statement that sets out the known limitations and conditions associated with the analysis." [V] (Ch 4, "4.2.1 Capacity"). The assurer (or the analyst) communicates the assurance state; the approver shall review the assurance evidence, be confident the work meets the design requirements and is of sufficient quality and proportionately documented, and follow governance for sign-off; the approver should challenge the analysts enough to gain assurance and give evidence of formal approval [AP] (Ch 9, "9.1.3"; "9.1.4"; "9.2.3 Sign-off"). Handover documentation may include the test plan and test results, change and version control logs, the limits of use and a statement of assurance (Ch 9, "9.3 Documentation").

12. <!-- concept: sunset-date-and-continuous-review --> **Continuous review, a sunset date, and openness when things go wrong.** "The analytical lifecycle is not a linear process." [V]: analysis in ongoing use should be regularly re-checked, including whether relied-on software is still supported and up to date, under robust version control (Ch 5, "5.3 Maintenance and continuous review"). Delivery evidence may include a sunset date, "a date beyond which the analysis and / or the model should not be used" [V] (Ch 9, "9.2.1 Delivery"), and "Model effectiveness can change over time." [V] through drift (Ch 9, "Regularly reviewing model health"). Senior leaders should build processes for reporting when things go wrong and reviewing failures in the assurance process; a box describes a department that reviewed internally why its assurance missed an error and published an external independent review [AE] (Ch 4, "4.1 Leadership"; "An open culture when things go wrong").

## Questions to Ask During Warranting Agent-Built Software

### Phase 1: Specifying the change

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Shared understanding | Have the client and the builder agreed, in writing, the question this change answers, its context and its boundaries, before the agent starts? | Ch 6, "Engagement and scoping"; "6.1.2 The analyst’s responsibilities" |
| Required assurance | Does the spec state the acceptable level of risk and the level of assurance this change needs, and has the client signed that off? | Ch 6, "6.1.2"; "6.1.1 The commissioner’s responsibilities" |
| Measurable acceptance | Are acceptable accuracy, precision and margins of error agreed for the outputs, so the reviewer has something to validate against? | Ch 6, "6.2 Assurance activities"; "6.3 Documentation" |
| Users | Who will use the result, and will they be involved in checking it meets their needs? | Ch 8, "8.2.1 Verification and validation" |
| Opaque parts | Does the change put an AI model in the product? If so, has the scoping discussed the risks and whether such a model is appropriate for this problem at all? | Ch 6, "6.5 Black box models" |
| Plan iteration | Has the design been iterated with the client, as the book expects, or did the agent's first plan become the plan? | Ch 7, "Design" |

### Phase 2: Triaging risk

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Business risk | If this change is wrong, what is the effect (money, operations, reputation, the public), and how likely is an error? Where does that put it: high, medium, low, very low? | Ch 3, "3.2 Structured assessment of business risk and complexity"; Ch 2, "Business critical analysis" |
| Response | If the risk is high, what new assurance measure treats its likelihood, and if none, should the change be stopped or the risk moved elsewhere? If medium, has the client agreed to carry it? | Ch 3, "3.2", Table 3-3 |
| Factors | Is the approach novel, a reuse of something built for another purpose, long-lived, or run repeatedly? Each changes what assurance the change needs | Ch 3, "3.1 Factors for determining appropriate assurance", Table 3-1 |
| Building up | For a high-risk change, are the basic checks still in place beneath the outside review, or has one replaced the other? | Ch 3, "3.1" |
| Proportion | Is a simple, low-influence change being run through months' worth of assurance? | Ch 3, "3.1" |
| AI in the product | For an LLM call or agent tool in the product, has the same structured risk assessment been done, with the right mix of experts and a view of what mitigations exist? | Ch 3, "3.4 Black-box models and business risk" |

### Phase 3: Locking the tests

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Planned first | Was the verification and validation planned at design, and did the reviewer review that plan before the build? | Ch 7, "7.1.2"; "7.1.3 The assurer’s responsibilities"; "7.2 Assurance activities" |
| Independent baseline | For complex behaviour, are the tests baselined against independent reference cases, not against the build's own output? | Ch 7, "7.2 Assurance activities" |
| Tests of the tests | Has anyone verified that the automatic tests actually check the behaviour they claim to? | Ch 8, "8.5 Black box models" |
| Plan changes | If the tests or the plan changed during the build, was the change raised with the client, recorded with who made it and why, and fed back to the reviewer? | Ch 8, "8.1.1"; "8.1.2"; "8.1.3"; Ch 2, "Decisions log" |
| Integration | Where the change touches several modules, is there a test suite that checks they still fit together, as well as each module alone? | Ch 7, "7.6 Multi-use models"; Ch 8, "8.6 Multi-use models" |
| Technique mix | Which classes of verification does this change get: static checks, dynamic tests, constraint checks such as assertions and boundaries? | Ch 8, "8.2.1 Verification and validation" |

### Phase 4: Building in the sandbox

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Records as you go | Is the ledger written during the build (assurance done, changes, decisions, assumptions), or reconstructed from the agent's closing summary? | Ch 5, "5.2.3 Analysis"; Ch 8, "Analysis" |
| Assumptions | Which assumptions did the agent make that nobody signed off? | Ch 2, "Assumptions log"; Ch 8, "8.3 Documentation" |
| Drift from design | Has the build moved away from the agreed design, and has the client reviewed that change? | Ch 8, "8.1.1 The commissioner’s responsibilities"; "8.1.2" |

### Phase 5: Gating deterministically

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Repeatable | If the gate is run again, are the results as expected? | Ch 1, "1.3.5 Analysis with RIGOUR" |
| Repeat runs | For a pipeline that runs repeatedly, is each run's version, data and parameters on record and checked? | Ch 3, "3.1", Table 3-1 |
| Code practice | Has the build followed the agreed code practice proportionately, and has the reviewer checked that it did? | Ch 8, "8.2.3 Assurance of code" |
| Shortfall | Was any gate skipped, and if so does the assurance statement say so, with the known limitations? | Ch 4, "4.2.1 Capacity" |

### Phase 6: Reviewing independently

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Independence | Is the reviewer independent of the build, and is the separation in proportion to the change's importance and complexity? | Ch 3, "Proportionality" |
| Both layers | Did the build do its own assurance, and did an independent reviewer also assure it? | Ch 3, "Proportionality"; Ch 5, "5.1" |
| Reviewer's work | Did the reviewer only read the build's assurance, or also carry out further verification and validation of its own? | Ch 8, "8.1.3 The assurer’s responsibilities" |
| Competence | Is the reviewer skilled and competent for this change, and qualified to assure the method if it changed mid-build? | Ch 4, "4.2.1 Capacity"; Ch 8, "8.1.3" |
| Findings | Has the build acted on each reported error or explained why not, and has the reviewer re-reviewed? | Ch 5, "5.1"; Ch 8, "8.1.2"; "8.1.3" |
| Challenge | Has anyone challenged the result, or did review end in quick agreement? | Ch 1, "1.3.5 Analysis with RIGOUR"; Ch 9, "9.1.4" |

### Phase 7: Warranting the change

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Evidence | Am I reviewing the assurance evidence (records, test results, the reviewer's confirmation), or the agent's account of it? | Ch 9, "9.1.4 The approver’s responsibilities"; "9.3 Documentation" |
| Assurance state | Has the reviewer confirmed the change was scoped, built, validated, verified and documented? | Ch 9, "9.1.3 The assurer’s responsibilities" |
| Limits | Does the pack say what was not assured, the known limitations, and what the change cannot be used for? | Ch 4, "4.2.1"; Ch 9, "9.3" |
| Risk level | Is any remaining risk high, or medium without the client's agreement? | Ch 3, "3.2", Table 3-3 |
| Accountability | Who is the one person accountable for each role on this change, and is there documentation a future maintainer could work from? | Ch 5, "5.1"; Ch 2, "User and technical documentation" |
| Expiry | Is there a date or condition after which this should be reviewed or no longer used? | Ch 9, "9.2.1 Delivery" |

### Phase 8: Releasing and operating

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Review cadence | Who re-checks this in use (inputs, supported software, calibration), and how often? | Ch 5, "5.3 Maintenance and continuous review" |
| Model health | For an AI component in the product, who reports its health to the client, and what would show drift? | Ch 9, "9.5"; "Regularly reviewing model health" |
| Scope creep | Is anyone using this for a purpose outside the one it was specified for? | Ch 9, "9.6 Multi-use models" |
| Failure | When something went wrong, did we review why the assurance missed it, and share the lesson? | Ch 4, "4.1 Leadership"; "An open culture when things go wrong" |

## What to Look For

| Signal | Diagnosis | Follow-up |
|---|---|---|
| The only review of the change was done by the session that built it, or by the builder who directed that session | No formal independent assurance; the analyst and assurer roles have been combined, which the book says shall not happen in any case (Ch 5, "5.1") | Route the change to a reviewer outside the build before it reaches the pack |
| A reviewer pass is recorded, but it only re-read the build's own test report | The assurer reviews the analyst's assurance *and* carries out further verification and validation as they see fit (Ch 8, "8.1.3") | Ask the reviewer for its own checks: a test of its own, a run against reference cases, a validation against the spec |
| The spec says what to build but not how sure we need to be | The specification should state the acceptable level of risk and the required level of assurance (Ch 6, "6.1.2") | Add both before the build, and have the client sign off |
| A high-risk change has an outside review on the pack but no basic tests | Interventions taken in isolation; they should build on each other (Ch 3, "3.1") | Put the low-risk checks back underneath the outside review |
| A trivial change waits days in the same gates as a risky one | Assurance out of proportion (Ch 3, "3.1") | Grade the change; lighter gates for very low risk, logged as a decision |
| Gates were skipped for a deadline and the pack reads as complete | Insufficient assurance not acknowledged, against a "should" (Ch 4, "4.2.1") | Add the shortfall and its known limitations to the pack, and tell the client what risk remains (Ch 3, "3.2") |
| The ledger is written after the build from the agent's summary | Records not produced throughout the work, against a "shall" (Ch 5, "5.2.3") | Rebuild the ledger from the session log and tool runs; make it write-as-you-go for the next change |
| The pack names no owner for each role, only *the agent* or *the team* | No single accountable individual per role (Ch 5, "5.1") | Name the client contact, the build owner, the reviewer and the signer |
| An LLM call in the product was triaged like ordinary code | The black-box guidance asks for the same structured risk assessment, a judgement on whether such a model is appropriate, and planned automatic checks (Ch 3, "3.4"; Ch 6, "6.5"; Ch 7, "7.5") | Reopen triage for that component and plan its output checks and monitoring |

## When to Use This Reference

Reach for this source when:

- The question is who has to assure a change and what the signer signs on: the division between doing the work, assuring it independently, and approving on evidence.
- The question is how much assurance a change needs, and what to do with a risk at each level (the risk matrix and its responses).
- Time has run out before assurance has, and the pack must say so honestly.
- The client's product includes an AI model, LLM call or agent tool, where the book's black-box guidance applies nearly as written.
- A system in ongoing use needs a review cadence, a sunset date or a check for drift.

Reach elsewhere for security requirements and threat classes (`owasp-asvs-5-0`, `owasp-llm-top10-2026`, `owasp-agentic-top10-2026`, `nist-ssdf-1-1`), for sandboxing and agent permissions (`openssf-finding-fixing-vulnerabilities-ai`, `owasp-agentic-threats-mitigations`), for the code practices the book delegates (`uk-duck-book-qa-of-code`), for executable acceptance criteria (`cucumber-bdd-gherkin`, `microsoft-code-with-engineering-playbook`), and for measured evidence on agents (`egashira-testsuitebench-2026`, `jimenez-swe-bench`, `becker-metr-ai-developer-productivity-2025`, `he-cursor-velocity-complexity-2025`). This source is guidance for government analysis; it states requirements and recommendations and gives departmental examples, but carries no measured evidence on software or agents.

## Worked Example

A two-person firm uses coding agents to build a change for a housing charity: incoming tenant messages are summarised by an LLM call and sorted into routine and urgent, so that urgent ones (a gas smell, no heating, a safety threat) reach a caseworker within the hour. The agent reports the change done with tests green. The accountable builder did not read the diff.

**Scoping.** The builder and the charity's operations lead write the spec together. *Transfer:* the charity is the commissioner, so the spec states the question, the boundaries (the change sorts messages; it does not reply to tenants), and the acceptable error: for urgent messages, no more than one miss in the reference set, with misroutes of routine messages tolerated (Concept 8; Ch 6, "6.2 Assurance activities"). Because the change puts an AI model in the product, the scoping covers whether such a model is appropriate for this problem at all, and the charity signs off a version that keeps a keyword rule running alongside the model (Ch 6, "6.5 Black box models").

**Triage.** The book's frame:

> "Business risk should be viewed as the combination of the potential effect of analytical errors and the likelihood of errors occurring. In situations where the risk is high, it is more important to reduce likelihood of errors than the level of the effect."
> (Ch 3, "3.2 Structured assessment of business risk and complexity")

A missed safety report is a severe effect, and an LLM's likelihood of misreading an unusual message is not low, so the change scores high. High risk should not be tolerated, and new assurance measures must be considered (Concept 3; Ch 3, "3.2", Table 3-3). *Transfer:* here the effect can be lowered too, which the book's setting rarely allows: the keyword rule means a miss by the model is not by itself a miss by the system. The builder records both treatments, likelihood and effect, on the ledger.

**Tests and review.** The agent's tests check that urgent-looking test messages come back urgent, but the session log shows the agent wrote them after the code from messages it composed itself. The book asks for complex behaviour to be tested "ideally with tests baselining their response against independent reference cases" [V] (Ch 7, "7.2 Assurance activities"). The operations lead supplies 200 real past messages, anonymised and labelled by caseworkers, as the reference set. The review goes to a reviewer agent run fresh, with read-only tools, outside the build session:

> "The roles of analyst and assurer shall be distinct from each other. The analyst should carry out their own assurance but responsibility for formal assurance to the approver and commissioner lies with the assurer."
> (Ch 5, "5.1 Roles and responsibilities")

The reviewer does not stop at the agent's report: it runs the reference set itself (further verification and validation, Ch 8, "8.1.3 The assurer’s responsibilities") and finds three urgent messages sorted as routine, all written without the words the tests used. *Transfer:* the build's green suite was verification against the build's own idea of urgent; the reference set is validation against what caseworkers call urgent (Concept 4). Two of the three are caught by the keyword rule; one, a tenant describing a partner's threats in indirect terms, is caught by neither.

**Sign-off.** The builder, as approver, reviews the evidence, not the diff: the signed spec, the risk score and its treatments, the reviewer's run of the reference set, and the open miss (Concept 11; Ch 9, "9.1.4 The approver’s responsibilities"). The remaining risk is still high on that class of message, so it is not tolerated: the change ships with a third treatment the charity agrees to, routing any message the model marks low-confidence to a person. The pack's assurance statement names the known limitation (indirect descriptions of threats), the date for a re-run of the reference set on fresh messages, and the condition under which the model should no longer be used (Concept 12; Ch 9, "9.2.1 Delivery"). Each role has a named person: the operations lead as commissioner, the second builder as owner of the build, and the signer.

## Anti-patterns This Reference Helps Avoid

- **The builder as their own assurer.** Signal: the person who wrote the prompts and steered the agent also signs the review. Diagnosis: the analyst and assurer roles shall be separate in all cases, even on quick work (Ch 5, "5.1"). Follow-up: the builder may approve; a reviewer outside the build assures.
- **Assurance as verification alone.** Signal: *all tests pass* is the whole case for the change. Diagnosis: assurance is more than checking against the specification; validation asks whether it fits the purpose, with users involved (Ch 1, "1.3.3"; Ch 8, "8.2.1"). Follow-up: add a validation step against the client's own cases.
- **The independent review that replaced the build's own checks.** Signal: *the reviewer will catch it*, so the build skips its tests. Diagnosis: independence adds formal assurance on top of the analyst's own; it does not replace it (Ch 3, "Proportionality"). Follow-up: require both on the ledger.
- **One-size gates.** Signal: every change gets the same gates whatever its risk, either all heavy or all light. Diagnosis: assurance should be proportionate to risk and complexity, and months of assurance on simple, low-influence work is out of proportion (Ch 1, "1.3.1"; Ch 3, "3.1"). Follow-up: grade each change at triage and record the grade.
- **The silent shortfall.** Signal: the deadline came first and the pack does not mention what was skipped. Diagnosis: insufficient assurance should be acknowledged in the assurance statement with its known limitations, and under constraint the areas of greatest risk come first (Ch 4, "4.2.1"; Ch 3, "3.2"). Follow-up: list the shortfall and tell the client what risk remains.
- **Medium risk accepted on the builder's say-so.** Signal: a known medium risk ships and the client was never told. Diagnosis: medium risk should not be tolerated without the commissioner's agreement (Ch 3, "3.2", Table 3-3). Follow-up: get the client's agreement on the record, or treat the risk.
- **The ledger written at the end.** Signal: the record of the change is the agent's closing summary. Diagnosis: traceable records of assurance shall be produced throughout the work (Ch 5, "5.2.3"). Follow-up: record as the build runs.
- **Ship and forget.** Signal: no review date, no owner for the system in use, no sunset condition. Diagnosis: the life cycle is not linear, and ongoing use needs regular review and, where fitting, a sunset date (Ch 5, "5.3"; Ch 9, "9.2.1"). Follow-up: set the review cadence and the expiry condition at sign-off.

Named disagreement on independence below |

**Named tensions and disagreements.**

- *Review independence: pairing or an independent assurer.* `uk-duck-book-qa-of-code` strongly recommends pair programming as the most timely and practical review method, with the reviewer working beside the author. This book says the assurer and the analyst shall be independent and the roles shall be separate in all cases, while allowing the analyst to do their own assurance as well (Ch 3, "Proportionality"; Ch 5, "5.1"). A tension, not a contradiction, since the Duck Book also recommends external review for high-risk work. For the harness, a reviewer agent pairing with the build session is the Duck Book's review, not this book's independent assurance.
- *Who may do the independent check.* `nist-ssdf-1-1` lets design review be done by qualified people not involved in the design *and/or* by automated processes in the toolchain, so an automated check alone can satisfy it. This book asks for a formal independent assurer, skilled and competent, who confirms the assurance state to the approver (Ch 4, "4.2.1"; Ch 5, "5.1").
- *Self-attestation.* `cisa-secure-software-attestation-form` is by default signed by the producer's own chief executive or designee, with assessment by a third-party assessor organisation as an alternative, not a requirement. This book requires assurance independent of the analyst. The acts differ (a procurement attestation, the assurance of analysis), so the tension bites when a warranty pack offers the producer's own signature as its only assurance.

## Citation and Source-Integrity Notes

**Borrowed-through gaps.** The book cites a large body of prior work [BT]: wider government standards for analysis, risk and public money; guidance on uncertainty, data quality, model review and AI assurance; a review of verification techniques from which it takes its six classes; problem structuring methods; and publication standards. None is held in this corpus, and this distillation names none of them. The one it relies on for code, the Duck Book, is held here as `uk-duck-book-qa-of-code`.

**Named limits of the source.** Written for UK government analysis and models: its roles assume a department with governance boards and senior leaders; its black-box guidance concerns AI models inside analysis, not coding agents; it carries no security, sandboxing or permission guidance and no measured evidence. Its risk weighting (likelihood over effect, because effect is usually beyond the analyst's control) is a claim about analysis; agent-built software can sometimes lower effect, and this distillation marks that as a transfer. The book says that "The AQuA Book, when final, will comply with the www.gov.uk accessibility statement." [V] ("Improving the book", "Accessibility"), implying a later revision is possible, which would be a re-projection trigger. The source carries some wording slips the deep reference records as found; none affects a claim used here.

**Evidence-marker continuity.** Every `[V]` quotation is copied from a `[V]` passage in the deep reference, which passed Pass I on 2026-10-15; the three blockquotes are the deep reference's Pass D key passages. The six verification technique classes are `[BT]` in the deep reference and stay `[BT]` here. The departmental example of an open review after an error is `[AE]`. Every *Transfer:* sentence is this distillation's inference from analysis assurance to agent-built software, not a claim the source makes; the role mapping in the setting paragraph is one such transfer. The modal verbs in paraphrases follow the deep reference, which kept the source's own.

## Runtime triggers this source addresses

| Trigger | Content from this source that addresses it | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|
| The story's acceptance criteria are prose ("works well", "handles errors") with no runnable check | The specification should state the acceptable level of risk and the required assurance; scoping agrees acceptable accuracy, precision and margins of error; the specification is the reference for later validation (Ch 6, "6.1.2"; "6.2"; "6.3") (Concept 8) | Put numbers on *works well*: what error is acceptable, and how sure we need to be. Without them the reviewer has nothing to validate against. |
| The agent is asked to "build X like Y" with no statement of what must not change | The specification captures the boundaries of the work (Ch 2, "Specification documentation"); reusing or repurposing existing work may need fresh verification and validation that the original method and assumptions still fit the new requirement (Ch 3, "3.1", Table 3-1) (Concept 2) | Write down where this change stops, and check that what made Y right still holds for X before you copy it. |
| Nobody can say who will use the change or what they will do with it | Engagement and scoping: commissioner and analyst develop a shared understanding of the problem and context; validation involves the users (Ch 6, "Engagement and scoping"; Ch 8, "8.2.1") (Concept 8) | Before the build, sit with the client until you can both say who uses this and for what; that is what validation will test. |
| The spec is long and the change is large | Larger projects may stage the work and return to design later (Ch 5, "5.2.2 Design"); modular work should assure each module and their integration (Ch 7, "7.6") | Stage it: specify and assure the first slice, and plan a check that the slices still fit together. |
| The builder says "the agent will figure out the details" | Black boxes place greater weight on design and on the validation of outputs by domain experts (Ch 7, "7.5") (Concept 10). *Transfer:* the agent's choices are opaque in the same way | What you can't inspect, you assure through the spec beforehand and the outputs afterwards; decide the details that matter now. |
| The change adds an LLM call, a prompt, a tool an agent can call, or memory | Black-box models get the same structured risk assessment; scoping discusses ethics and risks and whether such a model is appropriate; design plans automatic checks for unexpected behaviour and a maintenance plan (Ch 3, "3.4"; Ch 6, "6.5"; Ch 7, "7.5") (Concept 10) | This puts a black box in the product: score its risk on its own, ask whether a model is right for this job, and plan its output checks and monitoring now. |
| A migration, a delete or a bulk update is in the plan | Business risk is effect times likelihood; high risk should not be tolerated, and new assurance measures, then terminating or transferring the risk, must be considered (Ch 3, "3.2", Table 3-3) (Concept 3). A rehearsed rollback, which lowers the effect, is a harness rule, not the source's | Score the effect as severe; treat the likelihood with extra checks before it runs, and get the client's understanding on record if any risk stays. |
| The change is business-critical, or complex enough that nobody can predict its effects | Proportionate assurance; Table 3-1 factors; Figure 3-1 interventions scale with risk and complexity and build on each other (Ch 1, "1.3.1"; Ch 3, "3.1") (Concept 2) | Raise the assurance to match: more outside consultation, more separation between build and review, fuller records, on top of the basic checks, not instead of them. |
| The agent proposes changing a test so the build goes green | Changes to the plan are raised with the commissioner and documented; decisions are logged with who made and signed them off; the assurer gives feedback on changes to the plan (Ch 8, "8.1.1"; "8.1.2"; "8.1.3"; Ch 2, "Decisions log") (Concept 9). Locking the tests is a harness rule | A test change is a change to the plan: it needs a recorded reason, a named person who agreed it, and the reviewer's view. |
| The tests were written by the same agent session after the code | Verification and validation are planned at design and the assurer reviews the plan before the analysis; the analyst's own assurance is followed by the assurer's further verification and validation (Ch 7, "7.1.2"; "7.1.3"; Ch 8, "8.1.3") (Concept 7) | These tests are the build checking itself. The reviewer still has to check it independently, against cases the build didn't write. |
| The suite passes, but nobody knows whether it would catch a wrong implementation | Tests baselined against independent reference cases; verification of the automatic tests themselves (Ch 7, "7.2"; Ch 8, "8.5") | Test the tests: run them against reference cases with known answers, and see whether they would fail on a wrong one. |
| The agent runs for an hour unattended and reports success | Traceable documentation of assurance activities shall be produced throughout the analysis; the approver reviews assurance evidence, not the analyst's account (Ch 5, "5.2.3"; Ch 9, "9.1.4") (Concept 9) | A report of success isn't a record. Look for what was run, when, with what result, written down as it happened. |
| "It worked first time", or a flaky check passed on retry | Repeatable: if an approach is repeated the results should be as expected; an untried method needs more assurance, confidence growing as it is repeatedly tested (Ch 1, "1.3.5"; Ch 3, "3.1", Table 3-1) (Concept 5) | One pass is one run. Repeat it; if the result moves, the gate is telling you it can't yet be trusted. |
| A gate was skipped "just this once" | If time constraints mean insufficient assurance, this should be acknowledged in an assurance statement setting out known limitations (Ch 4, "4.2.1") (Concept 11) | If it's skipped, the pack says so and says what that leaves unchecked. |
| The same session that wrote the code reviews it | The assurer and the analyst shall be independent; the roles shall be separate in all cases (Ch 3, "Proportionality"; Ch 5, "5.1") (Concepts 6, 7) | The build can check its own work, and should, but that isn't the review. The rollback is a harness rule | Don't sign a risk nobody owns: name the owner, score it, and if it's medium or above get the client's agreement on record. |
